 Yusuff Ali's LuLu Group draws a firm line on fake news: What did the company say?
 The UAE-based retail group says it respects free speech but will continue pursuing legal action over what it describes as deliberate misinformation targeting its chairman and brand.
 Lulu Communications Director Nandakumar said the apology would not change the company's decision to pursue the legal proceedings
 ANI Photo
 By Teena Jose Nov 04, 2026 Teena Jose Teena Jose is a business journalist with around five years of experience covering business, technology and the people shaping today’s economy. She writes on companies, emerging trends, entrepreneurs and business leaders, with a particular interest in stories that connect business with wider social and economic change. Her work also includes in-depth profiles and interviews with industry leaders and changemakers.

 LuLu Group says it will not withdraw the legal cases filed over alleged misinformation. 
 Shajan Skariah has apologised to Yusuff Ali and reportedly acknowledged that some of his earlier allegations were incorrect. 
 The company says it supports freedom of expression but draws a distinction between criticism and what it calls deliberate falsehoods. 
 LuLu Group has said it will not withdraw its legal cases over alleged misinformation targeting its chairman, MA Yusuff Ali, despite an apology from Malayalam YouTuber Shajan Skariah.
 The UAE-based retail group says it respects freedom of speech and the right to question or criticize, but will not accept what it describes as deliberate false allegations intended to damage its reputation. The position was reiterated by LuLu Group Communications Director V Nandakumar in comments to the media on Monday (2) and Tuesday (3).
 “Zero Tolerance. No Compromise,” the company said in a statement, drawing a distinction between freedom of expression and the spread of misinformation.
 “Everyone has the right to an opinion. We respect freedom of speech, including the right to question, disagree and criticise. But deliberate false allegations, fake news and misinformation intended to malign cannot be passed off as a point of view,” it said.
 The statement also underlined the scale of the business and its workforce. LuLu described itself as a “home and a family” for more than 75,000 employees, saying their livelihoods, dedication and decades of trust were connected to the group's name.
 What did Shajan Skariah say in his apology?
 Skariah, founder of the Malayalam digital news platform Marunadan Malayalee, issued an apology to Yusuff Ali in a video published on October 31. He said he had realised that his earlier remarks were incorrect and was withdrawing them.
 The remarks related to a video published in November 2020 that made allegations against Yusuff Ali in connection with the gold smuggling case involving the UAE Consulate in Thiruvananthapuram. Skariah said he had not intended to personally insult or defame the LuLu chairman.
 The apology followed legal action initiated by Yusuff Ali over the allegations. The dispute has involved defamation proceedings, including a claim seeking Rs 10 crore in damages.
 Why is LuLu Group refusing to withdraw the cases?
 Nandakumar said the apology would not change the company's decision to pursue the legal proceedings. He told reporters that LuLu would not consider an out-of-court settlement and would rely on the Indian legal system to address the matter.
 The communications director also said cases had been filed in different places, not only in Kerala, and that the group would contest allegations against its chairman and brand through legal channels.
 For LuLu, the issue is not simply whether an apology has been made. Its public position is that criticism and disagreement are part of free expression, but claims it considers deliberately false should carry legal accountability.
 The company's statement repeated that it would not backtrack on the cases or withdraw them. The proceedings will therefore continue despite Skariah's public apology, leaving the courts to determine the legal issues.
 LuLu Group Communications Director V Nandakumar said the company would continue with the cases even if those accused of spreading false information apologised. He also ruled out an out-of-court settlement, saying the group had confidence in India's legal system. 
 The company's position is that an apology does not automatically bring the dispute to an end. It wants the allegations addressed through the legal process, rather than settled privately.
 LuLu Group International is a UAE-based conglomerate founded by Yusuff Ali, with interests spanning retail, shopping malls, food processing, wholesale distribution and hospitality. The company says it has more than 75,000 employees, a figure it invoked in its statement to underline the wider workforce behind its business and brand.
 For now, the group has made its position clear: it supports the right to question and criticize, but says it will pursue legal action over allegations it considers deliberately false. Skariah's apology has not changed that decision.

 Indian investors rush overseas for better returns as JioBlackRock and other fund managers launch global funds
 India Weekly Nov 06, 2026 GIFT City is a tax-neutral financial hub in Gujarat
 Sam Panthaky/ AFP/Getty Images
 Highlights: 
 At least six overseas funds have been launched in the past six months, including JioBlackRock’s Advantage World Equity Fund.
 International investments by Indian individuals more than doubled year-on-year to nearly $2.3 billion in the first half of 2026.
 India has more than 130 million retail stock investors, many seeking opportunities in overseas markets.
 GIFT City funds are not subject to the RBI’s existing overseas investment limits for domestic mutual funds.
 Overseas fund-of-funds assets rose 42 per cent year-on-year to ₹488 billion in September, with nearly two million registered investors.
 Industry executives have cautioned against investing abroad solely to chase short-term returns.
 INDIA’S top money managers are launching a flurry of funds in a tax-neutral hub to absorb the record sums that domestic investors are sending overseas, frustrated by weak returns at home and craving exposure to AI-related assets. 
 At least half a dozen such funds have been launched in the past six months, including the JioBlackRock Advantage World Equity Fund this week by the joint venture of Mukesh Ambani’s Jio Financial and BlackRock, the world’s largest asset manager. 
 The overseas investment rush poses a dilemma for policymakers, who have spent years encouraging households to move savings from real estate, gold and bank deposits into domestic equities. 
 The world’s most populous nation has more than 130 million retail stock investors, many of whom are scouring for investment targets abroad, from New York to Kazakhstan, after sustained underperformance in the domestic stock market.
 “Over the last two years, we’ve seen a clear increase in demand for global assets,” said Shobhit Mathur, co-founder of money manager Ionic Wealth. “Investors are no longer looking at overseas exposure as a tactical allocation but increasingly as a permanent part of portfolio construction.”
 International investments by individuals in India either directly or through funds more than doubled from a year earlier to nearly $2.3 billion in the first half of 2026, on track to surpass the 2025 full year’s record $2.65bn, data from the central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), showed. 
 One such investor is Ankit Khandelwal, a 41-year-old resident of Kota in Rajasthan, who invests in global exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and companies listed in markets such as Kazakhstan and Mongolia. 
 “It began as an experiment, but since then better returns overseas and persistent rupee weakness has led me to grow the overseas portion of my portfolio to over 60 per cent from about 5 per cent in early 2025,” said Khandelwal, who is an import and export adviser to companies, adding that he understands metals, mining and energy firms of the world.
 The RBI restricts Indian funds to a maximum cumulative overseas investment of $7bn and a $1bn limit for an individual asset manager. With the limits almost exhausted, funds cannot create fresh units to invest at will even as demand grows. 
 But these limits do not apply to overseas investment funds of domestic asset managers launched via the GIFT City tax-neutral hub in Gujarat. 
 Thus, besides JioBlackRock, HDFC Asset Management, Parag Parikh and Aditya Birla Sun Life have launched such funds in the past six months. Other domestic funds that invest in foreign equities too are sought after, despite the RBI limits. 
 Assets in overseas fund-offunds schemes rose 42 per cent year-on-year to `488bn in September, while investors registered for such investments climbed 34 per cent to nearly 2 million, according to data published by the Association of Mutual Funds in India.
 Indian authorities are cautious about the money flowing abroad from such investments but are not considering measures to curb such flows, three people at Indian regulators told Reuters. 
 Emails to India’s market regulator and the RBI, which sets overseas investment limits, were not answered. 
 Some industry executives voiced caution. “Indian markets have not given returns and overseas markets are looking attractive,” said Swarup Mohanty, chief executive of Mirae Asset Investment Managers. “If you want to invest for diversification then it’s fine, but investing purely to chase short-term returns is worrying.”

 Indian court orders removal of viral documentary accusing Modi and Adani of cronyism after defamation lawsuit
 India Weekly Nov 06, 2026 
 AFP/Getty Images
 Highlights: 
 Adani Enterprises sued Sabeer Bhatia, alleging that his documentary contained false and defamatory claims.
 The 36-minute film had attracted millions of views on social media.
 The court described the documentary as a “dramatized narrative”, rather than a news report.
 YouTube, X and Instagram have been directed to remove specified posts of the film until January 31, 2027.
 Bhatia said the lawsuit sought ₹500 million ($5.25 million) in damages and wrote: “Truth is on my side”.
 The documentary questions Adani Group's successful bids for six airports in 2019, which critics say followed changes to government rules that favoured the company.
 AN INDIAN court has ordered the removal of an online documentary accusing prime minister Narendra Modi and billionaire Gautam Adani (pictured) of cronyism after Adani Enterprises sued, calling the film defamatory. 
 The company told the high court in Kolkata that the documentary, posted by Hotmail co-founder Sabeer Bhatia, contained false content and had prompted inquiries from some investors. The film had garnered millions of views on social media in recent days. 
 The court’s order, issued late on Monday (26), described the documentary as “not a news report or an account of proceedings. It is a dramatized narrative.” 
 Adani Enterprises, Modi’s office, Bhatia and the social media companies did not respond to requests for comment. 
 In its legal challenge, Adani Enterprises said it did not seek to restrict constructive criticism of government policy or business concentration, but alleged that Bhatia had suppressed material facts, according to the court order. 
 Bhatia, who is based in the US, said on X that the lawsuit sought `500 million ($5.25 million) in damages.
 “Truth is on my side”, he wrote in one post.
 “I believe the documentary has rattled Adani Enterprises Limited and struck a nerve at the highest levels,” he wrote.
 Bhatia co-founded the once-popular email service Hotmail, which he sold to Microsoft in 1997.
 The court’s interim order, which remains in force until January 31, 2027, directs YouTube, X and Meta’s Instagram to remove several posts of the 36-minute film, The Friendship Files. It also bars Bhatia from distributing the video. Hearings are likely to resume in January. 
 On October 19, police in Maharashtra, which is governed by Modi’s ruling alliance, sent Bhatia a takedown notice, saying the content “made serious unsubstantiated allegations”. 
 The documentary uses archival footage to trace the relationship between Modi and Adani, who both come from the western state of Gujarat.
 It questions Adani’s successful bids for six airports in 2019 after a change in government rules that critics say favored the company. 
 The opposition Congress party has also raised similar allegations.
 The Adani group has denied the allegations, while the government has said all regulations were followed and there was no favoritism.
 Opposition figures have shared the documentary online. Regional leader Raj Thackeray, a Modi critic, removed it from his X account after it received 4.8 million views, saying he had acted at the request of the Mumbai police commissioner.

 Coca-Cola’s Indian bottling business eyes $1bn IPO at $10bn valuation
 Teena Jose Oct 27, 2026 Coca-Cola’s Indian bottling business is preparing for a potential public listing following an ownership restructuring in 2025
 iStock
 Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings is expected to file its draft prospectus with India’s market regulator by October 29. 
 The proposed IPO could raise around $1bn at a targeted valuation of approximately $10bn. 
 Coca-Cola owns 60 per cent of the business, while Jubilant Bhartia Group holds the remaining 40 per cent. 
 Coca-Cola’s Indian bottling business is moving closer to a potential stock market listing, with its parent company, Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings (HCCH), expected to file draft IPO papers with India’s market regulator this week.
 The proposed initial public offering could raise around $1bn, primarily through a stake sale, at a targeted valuation of approximately $10bn, according to media reports citing sources familiar with the plans. A listing is expected in 2027, although the timing and final terms remain subject to regulatory approvals and market conditions.
 HCCH is the parent company of Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages (HCCB), which manufactures, packages and distributes Coca-Cola products across India . Axis Capital and IIFL Capital Services are among the investment bankers expected to manage the offering, while Rothschild & Co has been appointed as an adviser to the listing process, according to the reports.
 The proposed IPO follows an ownership restructuring completed in July 2025, when Jubilant Bhartia Group acquired a 40 per cent stake in HCCH. The Coca-Cola Company retained the remaining 60 per cent.
 The listing would mark another step in Coca-Cola’s strategy of reducing its direct exposure to capital-intensive bottling operations while retaining control over its brands, marketing and product development.
 Why is Coca-Cola preparing to list its Indian bottler?
 The proposed offering reflects a broader shift in Coca-Cola’s business model towards working with independent bottling partners. Under this approach, the company can focus more on brand building, innovation and marketing while its bottlers handle manufacturing and distribution.
 The partnership with Jubilant Bhartia Group gives Coca-Cola a shareholder with established consumer-facing businesses in India. Jubilant FoodWorks operates brands including Domino’s Pizza, Popeyes and Dunkin’, creating potential opportunities across beverage distribution and quick-service restaurants.
 Coca-Cola executives have presented the proposed listing as an opportunity to support the bottler’s future growth. Jubilant Bhartia Group Chairman Shyam Bhartia and Co-Chairman Hari Bhartia have also expressed support for the partnership and the potential to create shareholder value.
 However, the proposed IPO's final structure, including the proportion of shares to be sold and the allocation between shareholders, has yet to be confirmed.
 A large distribution network, but revenue has come under pressure
 Established in 1997, HCCB operates 14 bottling plants across 10 Indian states and works with a network of more than 2,000 distributors, serving over 1.7 million customers. The company employs approximately 5,000 people and works with additional co-packers to support production.
 Despite its scale, the business has faced pressure on revenue. HCCB reported revenue of ₹12,751.29 crore, equivalent to approximately $1.5bn, in the financial year ended March 2025, down 9 per cent year over year, according to company filings cited by Fortune India.
 The decline followed the transfer of manufacturing plants in Rajasthan, Bihar, the Northeast and parts of West Bengal to independent franchise bottlers. Those changes reduced the operations directly consolidated within HCCB, meaning the revenue decline should not automatically be interpreted as an equivalent fall in demand for Coca-Cola products .
 The beverage industry has also faced difficult trading conditions, with persistent and unseasonal rainfall affecting sales during the April-to-September period. The summer season typically accounts for a substantial share of annual soft drink consumption in India.
 In July 2025, HCCB appointed Hemant Rupani, formerly president for Southeast Asia at Mondelez, as chief executive, replacing Juan Pablo Rodriguez.
 The proposed IPO will give investors an opportunity to assess the bottling business as a standalone listed company. Its valuation will depend not only on its distribution reach and relationship with Coca-Cola, but also on its revenue performance, profitability and ability to grow under the revised operating model.

 Reliance’s Jio Platforms IPO set for market debut after $3.5bn share sale draws strong demand
 Teena Jose Oct 27, 2026 Reliance’s Jio Platforms is preparing to make its stock market debut after attracting strong demand for its $3.2 billion IPO.
 PRAKASH SINGH/AFP via Getty Images
 Jio Platforms’ $3.2 billion IPO was subscribed 22.19 times, led by institutional investors. 
 The shares are scheduled to begin trading on the BSE and NSE at 10 am local time on Wednesday (28). 
 An unofficial grey market premium of around $2.56 per share suggests a potential listing price about 21.8 per cent above the offer price, although the actual debut price could differ. 
 Reliance’s Jio Platforms is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday (28) after its $3.2 billion initial public offering attracted strong demand from investors, setting up a closely watched listing for one of India’s largest technology businesses.
 The IPO raised approximately $3.2 billion through a fresh issue of 270 million shares. It was subscribed 22.19 times overall during the bidding period, according to stock exchange data, with institutional investors accounting for the strongest demand.
 The shares are scheduled to list on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE) at 10 am local time. The listing follows a special pre-open session, during which investors can enter, modify or cancel orders before the exchanges match orders and determine the opening price.
 The offer price ranged from approximately $11.18 to $11.75 per share, based on the exchange rate on October 27. The minimum application was for 12 shares, requiring an investment of about $141 at the upper end of the price range.
 What drove demand for the Jio Platforms IPO?
 The IPO received an overall subscription of 22.19 times the shares available to investors, with qualified institutional buyers leading the demand.
 The institutional investor portion was subscribed 70.55 times, while the non-institutional investor category was subscribed 14 times. Retail investors subscribed 2.72 times their allocated portion.
 The issue attracted bids worth more than $51 billion, excluding the anchor investor placement, according to reported stock exchange data. Demand across the public offering and anchor investor placement was reported to exceed $77 billion.
 The IPO consisted entirely of newly issued shares, with no offer-for-sale component. This means the company is raising fresh capital rather than allowing existing shareholders to sell shares through the offering.
 Jio Platforms plans to use up to approximately $2.9 billion of the proceeds to repay certain outstanding borrowings of its subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm. The remaining funds are intended for general corporate purposes.
 The company said in its prospectus that it expected the listing to create a public market for its shares and deliver the benefits associated with being listed on the stock exchanges.
 Could Jio Platforms shares rise on debut?
 Jio Platforms shares were commanding an unofficial grey market premium of around $2.56 per share on October 27, according to IPO tracking websites.
 Adding that premium to the upper offer price of approximately $11.75 gives an indicative listing price of around $14.32 per share, or about 21.8 per cent above the issue price.
 At that indicative price, an investor allotted one lot of 12 shares would hold stock worth approximately $172, representing a paper gain of around $31 before transaction costs and taxes.
 However, the grey market premium is not an exchange-published price or a reliable guarantee of listing performance. It reflects informal trading and expectations before the shares begin regular trading, and can change with market sentiment and broader market conditions.
 The actual opening price could be higher or lower than the estimate. Investors will have a clearer indication of market demand once the exchanges complete their pre-open process and regular trading begins.
 The listing is an important milestone for Reliance’s telecom and digital business, which has become a significant part of the group’s technology ambitions. The market debut will give investors a direct way to trade shares in Jio Platforms and assess its valuation against expectations for future growth.
 Strong IPO demand has raised expectations, but the first trading session will determine whether that enthusiasm translates into a sustained market premium.

 Ambani’s Jio Platforms IPO oversubscribed 3.16 times on day one
 India Weekly Oct 21, 2026 The telecom business, led by Ambani’s son Akash, launched in 2016 on a bet that Indians would use far more internet data if it were almost free. 
 Reuters
 Jio Platforms’ $3.2 billion IPO fully booked in under two hours
 Offering subscribed 3.16 times on day one
 IPO values Ambani’s telecom giant at up to $108.3 billion
 Shares to start trading October 28
 INVESTORS rushed to buy into Jio Platforms’ $3.2 billion initial public offering Wednesday, with bids covering all the shares on offer in under two hours, in India’s largest IPO and the first by Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance in 20 years.
 By the end of the first day, the offering was subscribed 3.16 times. Institutional investors filled their allotted portion in 10 minutes, and the overall book was covered within 100 minutes, two people close to the IPO told Reuters.
 “It’s the fastest in the history of India,” one said.
 The IPO values Jio Platforms at up to $108.3 billion, potentially making it one of India’s most valuable companies when trading begins October 28. Rival Bharti Airtel had a market value of $123.38 billion Wednesday.
 A rare fast start 
 Big Indian IPOs usually start slowly, with institutions often waiting until the final hours to bid. The National Stock Exchange of India’s recent share sale was only 42 percent subscribed on its first day, and Hyundai Motor India’s just 18 percent.
 Reliance says it welcomes Starlink competition as both await security clearance in India 
 “Jio has changed India’s telecom landscape and (the IPO) offers a very reasonable valuation with strong fundamentals,” said Aishvarya Dadheech, founder of Fident Asset Management.
 Institutions have so far shown far more enthusiasm than retail investors. Qualified institutional buyers bid for 9.42 times their reserved portion, while retail investors, who are allotted around a third of the issue, bid for 0.73 times theirs. The pace of new bids slowed after the early morning rush, exchange data showed.
 Earlier this week, Jio allotted shares worth $853 million to more than 200 anchor investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and BlackRock, after the reserved portion drew bids of more than $25 billion.
 The offering closes Friday, with shares priced at 1,065 to 1,119 rupees (about $11 to $11.60) each.
 India’s telecom giant 
 Backed by Meta, Google and institutional investors, Jio Platforms owns India’s largest telecom company, with more than 500 million subscribers. That makes it the world’s second-largest telecom operator in a single country after China Mobile.
 The telecom business, led by Ambani’s son Akash, launched in 2016 on a bet that Indians would use far more internet data if it were almost free. It quickly took market share from rivals such as Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea with cheap data and free voice calls.
 Almost 90 percent of Jio’s revenue comes from telecom. The company earned about $3.2 billion in profit on $15.5 billion in revenue in the year to March.
 Up to $2.89 billion of the proceeds will be used to repay debt at its telecom unit, with the rest going to general corporate purposes, including capital spending.
 A long-awaited listing 
 Ambani first promised a Jio listing in 2019. The plans were delayed in 2025, and a filing for as early as March was pushed back after the Iran war dampened appetite for IPOs.
 Jio is chasing India’s biggest IPO yet 
 Jio is launching the offering during the Hindu festive season, considered an auspicious time for purchases, though Indian markets have been subdued in recent weeks.
 Reliance paid its more than 400,000 employees about 15 days early this month and helped people open share-trading accounts ahead of the IPO, a person with direct knowledge of the matter said. Reliance did not respond to a request for comment.
 For many Indian families, Reliance shares have long been a source of savings for education and weddings. Its Mumbai-traded stock has risen around 330-fold since 1990.
 (With inputs from Reuters)
